strengths: The paper has a clear structure, and it‘s easy to follow.
The idea of modeling the head and shoulder separately is interesting. The neural texture strategy can model the shoulders efficiently with less 3D Gaussians.
The pipeline is verified on different human subjects.
The paper is well written and easy to follow.
The use of a neural texture map to model the shoulders is well motivated and intuitive.
The additional loss terms introduced are well ablated in both the main paper and the supplementary.
The proposed method both qualitatively and quantitatively outperforms prior work.
This paper uses neural textures to model body parts simultaneously, instead of just the head.
The paper proposes a method to accelerate reasoning, so that the rendering speed can reach 130 frames per second.
This method effectively models detailed upper body textures.
This paper combines 3DGS and neural fields to construct head and body textures, showcasing technical novelty.
Experimental results demonstrate that this method has significant advantages in rendering accuracy and inference speed while using a smaller number of 3D Gaussians.
The overall writing is easy to following and well-written.

It seems like compared with conventional method, which ignore the shoulder but only focus on face, this model presents better performance and more robust to shoulder renderings (like compare with PointAvatar and GS*)
weaknesses: The method models head and shoulders separately, i.e., different Gaussian representations and different tracking approaches. This causes a limitation, i.e., the head and shoulders are misaligned for some relatively big body movements.
It seems that the Anchor Gaussian only supports relatively simple shoulder motions. It’s not verified that the proposed method can model pose-dependent wrinkles for the shoulders in the paper.
The body movements in the supplementary demo are too simple, and I cannot observe that the clothing wrinkles vary with poses.

There are no significant out-of-plane view synthesis results that are shown in the results to demonstrate whether or not the learned texture map is able to generate novel renders of the shoulders in a geometrically consistent way or it just renders them as a plane.

This paper is, I believe, a little out of scope of ICLR and is more suited at a vision or graphics conference. However, I will defer to other reviewers and the AC for that before I consider it as a strong weakness.

There is no ablation of exactly how robust the proposed method is to shoulder movement in the capture video. Understanding this would help evaluate the method more thoroughly (I do grant that prior work does not even address this problem, but I believe this is important to make the paper more complete).
Any reason why Splatting-avatar results are so much worse compared to the other methods?
This paper lacks comparisons with some methods in terms of head reconstruction quality, including [1, 2].
The head part of this method is similar to the theory of existing methods (PSAvatar).

The tracking results given in Figure 11 are not convincing. In many body tracking projects, some scenes containing half of the body can still produce reasonable results. The paper should describe in more detail the methods used for tracking and why they were failed, otherwise I don't see the point why not using the upper body SMPL model.
The article lacks some clarity in its writing. For example, it does not explain what texture space is in the introduction.
The article could include additional baselines, such as Gaussian Avatars and Gaussian Head Avatar.

Regarding the rendering formula in Section 3.5, the coefficient for the third term, body texture, is the product of the opacities of the first two terms. Wouldn't this cause most of the pixels' colors in the third term to be overridden?
The author did not include Real3D-Portrait and StyleAvatar (joint face and shoulder rendering works) in the comparison.
The videos in the supplementary material do not present very large shoulder motions, making it unclear whether the model is robust in rendering the shoulder.
Missing ablations for the main method components such as anchor gaussians for shoulder only, the 3d-2d correspondence, and the neural texture compared with baseline GS and PointAvatar.
